newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Legal headaches to plague Brazil's CVRD for years.
newsitem.headline: Legal headaches to plague Brazil's CVRD for years.

text.p: Legal headaches will plague the new owners of Brazilian mining giant CVRD for years, but they do not threaten to reverse Tuesday's successful auction of the mammoth federally-owned company, legal experts said.
Just moments after the hammer came down on the 3.3 billion real ($3.1 billion) sale, a judge issued an injunction that suspended the transfer of CVRD shares to a group led by Brazil steelmaker CSN.
But that injunction, like dozens of others expected to be filed over the next several years, should be easily overturned and is not seen as a cause for alarm, attorneys said.
"An injunction by nature is a very feeble thing," said Marcelo Muriel, a partner at Sao Paulo-based law firm Pinheiro Neto.
"People think an injunction can solve all their problems, but it takes just a couple of minutes to overturn one. You wouldn't want your life to depend on one," Muriel added.

Attorneys and high court justices said it could take anywhere from two to 10 years to hear all the legal challenges to CVRD. But in the end, the courts were seen ruling in favor of the sale. And in the meantime, CSN was expected to take full control of the huge mining operation.
Attorneys point out that the courts have not always sided with the Brazilian government and its drive to reform Latin America's largest economy.
In February, Brazil's Supreme Court ruled in favor of state workers in a back-pay dispute that could cost the federal goverment up to $20 billion over the next five years.

Still, legal analysts said that in all of the cases in which the courts have sided against the government, judges had firm legal ground on which to base their ruling. That is not the case with the CVRD injunctions, they said.

"All of these injunctions are groundless. Opponents of the CVRD sale are turning the courts into a political arena as a last resort because they have already lost in Congress and in the press," said a Brazilian attorney who asked not to be named.

Legal challenges, which delayed the auction of CVRD by one week, have ranged from questions about the constitutionality of privatizing state companies to the way in which the government publicized the auction.
Government privatization officials were careful not to discredit the latest legal hurdle and said they would seek to overturn it today. But they appeared confident that the auction was a done deal.
Speaking on a morning television news program, CSN President Benjamin Steinbruch said he saw no serious obstacle to the group taking over CVRD.
But opponents of the sale remain determined to put CVRD back in government hands.

"There is still a chance we can annul the auction," said Othon de Azevedo, an attorney representing law professor Celso Antonio Bandeira de Mello, who was granted an injunction that delayed the sale of CVRD for a full week.
De Mello launched three new legal challenges following the auction on Tuesday of a 41.7 percent stake in CVRD. He is awaiting a decision from Brazil's Superior Justice Tribunal.

A flood of legal action was also expected to accompany the next two phases of CVRD's privatization, when the government sells a five percent stake in the company to CVRD employees and when it carries out a global offering of its remaining stake in CVRD.
